Family Health

Using a tampon: insertion, removal and swimming safely

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Tampons are one optional way to manage menstrual flow. Learning the parts and following your own product's instructions can make insertion and removal clearer, but pain is a reason to stop: not something you have to practise enduring. Pads and period underwear remain valid choices whether or not you ever use tampons.

Know which part stays inside

The absorbent tampon sits in the vagina, below the cervix, and takes up menstrual flow. Its removal string stays outside the vaginal opening. Some products come inside an applicator: a wider outer tube holds the tampon and an inner plunger releases it. The applicator is removed after insertion; it does not stay in the body.

Tampons may be made from cotton, rayon or a mixture; applicators may be plastic or cardboard. Read the packaging for the actual product. FDA-authorized tampons use an elemental-chlorine-free bleaching process, but this does not certify every product sold worldwide. Use a new single-use tampon each time; do not wash and reuse it. An external pad or period underwear can provide optional backup for leaks.

Choose the lowest absorbency you need

Light, regular and super describe absorbency, not how experienced you are. Choose the lowest level that manages your flow within the product's changing instructions. Your needs may change during a period, without a rule that a certain day always requires a certain size. If a tampon remains mostly dry after hours, a lower absorbency or external product may be more suitable.

FDA advice is to change every four to eight hours and never leave one in longer than eight hours; change sooner if needed or if the label says so. Being able to leave it in for eight hours without a change can mean absorbency is too high, not that you should increase it. In the US test system, 'super' means more than 9 up to 12 grams of standardized test fluid. That is not a guarantee of how much menstrual blood it will hold for you, or permission to wait until it is full.

Prepare without rushing

Use tampons only during menstrual bleeding, not for daily discharge or dry practice. Wash and dry your hands, check the wrapper is intact and open a fresh product. Discard one dropped onto a dirty surface. Read the instructions before using it: some compact applicators need extending, while others are ready to use. Do not push the tampon out of its applicator in advance unless its instructions require that preparation.

Choose a stable comfortable position, such as sitting on the toilet or standing with one foot on a secure low support. A mirror can help identify the vaginal opening between the urethral opening and anus. Take your time and breathe normally. Relaxing may help, but difficulty is not a personal failure, and you do not have to keep trying when it hurts.

Inserting a tampon with an applicator

Hold the applicator at its grip, keeping the removal string free. With the other hand, gently separate the labia and place the rounded tip at the vaginal opening. Guide it slowly towards your lower back, along the vaginal canal, rather than straight upwards towards your abdomen. Insert only as directed for that applicator, commonly until the fingers at the grip reach the opening; stop if there is pain or resistance.

Hold the outer tube steady and press the inner plunger as the instructions show to release the absorbent tampon. Gently remove the whole applicator, leaving only the tampon inside and its string outside. Put the applicator and wrapper in a bin and wash your hands. Do not leave either tube inside, pull the string immediately after placement, or insert a second tampon.

Inserting a tampon without an applicator

With clean hands, unwrap the product, free the string and check it as the label describes. Hold the base with your thumb and middle finger and place your index finger at the base. In a comfortable position, gently separate the labia with your other hand and place the tampon at the vaginal opening.

Guide it gently backwards along the canal with your index finger, following the product's directions until it rests comfortably; leave the string outside. Remove your finger and wash your hands. Do not aim forwards, force it against resistance or assume you must push to a fixed finger depth. If you cannot place it comfortably, remove it if possible and choose another product while seeking advice.

Comfort matters more than another attempt

A correctly placed tampon should not cause pain or ongoing awareness. Discomfort can relate to placement, dryness or absorbency, but it can also have another cause. Stop and gently remove it rather than repeatedly pushing through pain. If you choose to try again later, use a fresh tampon and the lowest suitable absorbency while you are bleeding.

A small amount of suitable water-based vaginal lubricant on the tip may help if compatible with the product; a pharmacist can advise. Do not substitute petroleum jelly, perfumed creams or household oils. Persistent pain, inability to insert or painful removal should be discussed with a clinician. It does not automatically diagnose a vaginal septum, and a more absorbent tampon is not the answer to every difficulty.

The string and ordinary removal

Leave the string outside and do not cut it or deliberately tuck it into the vagina. When it is time to change, wash your hands and sit or stand comfortably. Relax the pelvic muscles as much as you can, hold the string and draw the tampon out slowly and gently. Do not yank or keep pulling against significant pain.

Wrap the used tampon and put it in a rubbish bin; do not flush it, its wrapper or an applicator. Wash your hands afterwards and check that the old tampon is out before using a new one. Remove the last tampon at the end of the period. Dry, difficult removal may indicate too much absorbency for that flow; it does not justify exceeding the maximum wearing time.

If the string is missing or a tampon seems stuck

A tampon cannot travel through the cervix into the uterus or disappear into the abdomen. It can sit higher in the vagina with its string out of reach. If you feel well, you can try one gentle removal attempt with clean hands: squat or sit, bear down gently as for a bowel movement, and see whether a clean finger can reach the tampon. If easily reachable, grasp it carefully with your fingers and draw it out.

If it does not come out easily, you are unsure whether one remains, or part seems retained, get prompt medical help. Do not use tweezers or another object, keep searching forcefully, insert another tampon or have vaginal penetration. Tell the clinician approximately how long it may have been present. New unpleasant smell, discharge, pelvic pain or urinary discomfort also needs assessment; illness or toxic-shock symptoms require immediate care.

Keep track of time, including overnight

Note the insertion time or set a reminder. Use the interval on the label, within the maximum of eight hours, and change earlier when necessary. A pad or period underwear is a sensible choice if you expect to sleep longer than the safe interval. Extra absorbency does not make a longer night safe.

If you realise it has been more than eight hours, remove it as soon as you can and pay attention to how you feel. Difficulty removing it needs prompt help. The time alone does not diagnose infection, but feeling unwell requires care and should not be watched at home while waiting for more symptoms. TSS can occur without a tampon having been worn beyond eight hours.

Swimming during your period

You can swim with a tampon if you want to and feel comfortable using it. It may absorb some water, so use a fresh one for swimming and change it shortly afterwards, following the label and usual time limits. Carry spares and arrange access to a changing space. Water does not pause the wearing-time clock.

A little absorbed water does not prove an infection has occurred. Swimming is not a reason to select more absorbency than your flow needs or force an uncomfortable tampon. If an internal product does not suit you, ask about alternatives designed for swimming, or choose another activity. Ordinary pads may become waterlogged; no product choice is a measure of maturity.

Urinating and sexual activity

Urine leaves through the urethra, a different opening from the vagina, so you do not need to remove a tampon just to urinate. Keep the string accessible outside and change the tampon when due. If the string gets wet or the product feels uncomfortable, you can replace it with a fresh one; washing hands remains important.

Remove a tampon before vaginal penetration with a penis or sex toy. Penetration can push it further in and make removal difficult. A tampon is for menstrual flow, not contraception or protection from sexually transmitted infections. Keep any needed contraception and infection prevention separate from menstrual-product choices.

Recognise toxic shock symptoms promptly

Toxic shock syndrome, or TSS, is rare but potentially life-threatening. It involves toxins made by certain bacteria and can occur with or without tampon use. Sudden fever, a rough or sunburn-like rash, vomiting or diarrhoea, marked muscle aches, dizziness or feeling faint during or soon after tampon use need immediate medical advice. Do not wait for all symptoms, a specific rash or more than eight hours of wear.

Remove the tampon if easily possible and tell the care team you were using one; inability to remove it must not delay help. Loss of consciousness, confusion, trouble breathing, a non-fading rash, or blue, grey, very pale or blotchy skin needs emergency care immediately. If you have previously had TSS, ask a clinician before using tampons again.

A brief history, and the choice today

Modern applicator designs have a long history: Earle C. Haas filed the application for US patent 1,926,900 in November 1931, and it was granted in September 1933. That historical document is not a guide to today's hygiene or disposal. Current product instructions and safety guidance matter more than how old a design is.

Tampons can be convenient for movement, swimming and clothing preferences, but they are not necessarily better than pads, cups or period underwear for everyone. Choose what feels comfortable and manageable, ask for help with questions, and seek care for pain or unusual symptoms rather than treating them as the price of learning.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Read your product's instructions and check the parts before insertion; use clean hands and stop if it hurts.

Record insertion time, use the lowest needed absorbency and plan changes within the label and eight-hour limit.

Choose a comfortable alternative when needed; get prompt help for retained products and immediate care for TSS warning signs.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record changing times, flow patterns and questions for an appointment. It cannot confirm tampon position, rule out a retained product or infection, or diagnose TSS. Do not wait for an app reminder or reassuring record when removal is difficult or you feel unwell.

When to seek help

Possible TSS symptoms during or soon after tampon use need immediate medical attention, even without every symptom or prolonged wear. Remove the tampon if easily possible without delaying help. Loss of consciousness, confusion, breathing difficulty, non-fading rash or blue, grey, very pale or blotchy skin requires emergency care. Get prompt clinical help if a tampon cannot be removed easily or may remain inside.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The tampon stays in the vagina, the string stays outside, and the whole applicator comes out.
  • Use the lowest needed absorbency, change as directed and never exceed eight hours.
  • Follow the exact product's insertion method; stop rather than force pain or resistance.
  • Swimming and urination are possible with a tampon; remove it before vaginal penetration.
  • Get help promptly for difficult removal and immediately for possible TSS or emergency symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Can a tampon get lost inside me?

It cannot pass into the uterus or abdomen. It may sit higher in the vagina with an inaccessible string. Try only gentle removal with clean fingers if easily reachable; get prompt help if it does not come out or you are unsure one remains. Do not use tools.

How long can I wear one?

FDA advice is four to eight hours, with earlier changes as needed or directed by the label. Never exceed eight hours, including overnight, and do not wait for saturation. Use an external product if you will sleep longer.

Can I swim with a tampon?

Yes, if it is comfortable and you want to. Use a fresh one and change shortly after swimming because it may absorb water. Keep the usual time limits; swimming does not require higher absorbency or painful insertion.

How much does a super tampon absorb?

In the US standardized test, super means more than 9 through 12 grams of test fluid. It is not a personal menstrual-blood measurement or a safe waiting target. Check your product's label and use the lowest absorbency needed.

Should insertion or removal hurt?

No. Stop, remove it gently if possible and use an external product. Persistent pain or difficulty needs clinical advice rather than force or repeated practice through pain. Not every difficulty means a structural abnormality.

Do I have to remove it to pee?

No. The urethra and vagina are separate openings. Keep the string outside and remember the usual changing time.

Can I have vaginal penetration with one in?

Remove it first. Penetration may push it higher and make removal harder. It does not prevent pregnancy or sexually transmitted infections.

What if I forgot it for more than eight hours?

Remove it as soon as possible. Seek prompt help if removal is difficult, and immediate medical care for sudden fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhoea, dizziness or other possible TSS symptoms. Do not wait for every symptom; loss of consciousness, confusion or breathing trouble is an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
